newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Moscow hails visit by Chinese leader.
newsitem.headline: Moscow hails visit by Chinese leader.

text.p: Moscow gave a warm welcome to Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Tuesday at the start of his five-day state visit to Russia to boost ties between the two giant neighbours.

Jiang, accompanied by his wife Wang Yeping and senior Chinese officials, was greeted by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin at the government airport and escorted to an apartment in the Kremlin -- a rare honour granted only to a few selected dignitaries in the past.

President Boris Yeltsin will briefly interrupt his holiday at the Black Sea resort of Sochi to offer a formal welcome to Jiang on Wednesday and sign with him a political declaration outlining a joint vision of the future world order.

"This will be the first Russian-Chinese summit after the two sides declared in Beijing in April 1996 their commitment to a new course of developing partnership aimed at strategic cooperation in the 21st century," Itar-Tass quoted Russian foreign ministry spokesman Gennady Tarasov as saying.
Jiang said in a written statement issued on his arrival that relations between Russia and China had an impact on processes wider than their bilateral relations.

"The establishment of a new type of bilateral relationship between China and Russia...not only serves the fundamental interests of our two peoples but also contributes to peace, stability and development in the Asian-Pacific region and in the world at large," the statement said.

Jiang, Yeltsin and the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan will also sign a treaty on reducing armed forces along the former Soviet-Chinese border. Details of the treaty have not been made public.
Moscow, wary of NATO's plans to expand eastwards, has made Jiang's visit a hugely symbolic event.

Jiang, who has a good knowledge of the Russian language and literature, will go on Friday to Yasnaya Polyana, the estate of writer and philosopher Leo Tolstoy about 200 km (130 miles) south of Moscow.
Moscow and Beijing have made clear they are poised to set an example for other countries on how to maintain security and build bilateral ties.

"This new type of relationship includes a refusal to take part in military blocs, ruling out confrontation and any menace to third parties," Interfax news agency quoted the Chinese ambassador to Moscow, Li Fenglin, as saying.

Yeltsin's spokesman, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, underlined the importance of the joint political declaration -- the first such document signed since Moscow and Beijing started repairing ties in the late 1980s after more than two decades of hostility.

"In this declaration...Russia and China will express their vision of how to form the new international order in the 21st century and will speak out against claims by any country to the role of absolute leader," he told Interfax.
He named no state but Moscow and Beijing have been critical of Washington's domination of the post-Cold War world order.

"The spirit of (Jiang's) visit is in sharp contrast to the tendencies emerging in the west such as NATO plans to expand," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Igor Rogachev, the Russian ambassador to China, as saying on Monday.

Moscow also hopes for better trade relations with Beijing that would bring greater access to the vast Chinese market and to markets in South-East Asia and the Pacific Rim. But it must solve some problems if the honeymoon with Beijing is to go on.
Tass news agency said two-way trade reached $6.9 billion in 1996, 25 percent up on 1995. But the balance is lop-sided in Russia's favour to the tune of about $3.5 billion.
Russian officials have said that trade turnover could reach $8-10 billion in 1997 and $20 billion by the end of the century.
